uni-bba-ob.description: Individual, group and organisation-level behaviour: personality, perception, learning, attitudes, motivation, leadership, groups and teams, conflict, power, culture and change, with Indian workplace cases. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BBA programmes.

lessons.title: What OB studies and why managers need it

scenes.text: A Bengaluru start-up pays its top developer Arjun well, yet he resigns after six months.
In the exit interview he says: my manager never listened and the team ignored my ideas.
Salary was not the problem. Behaviour was. That is the territory of Organisational Behaviour.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Organisational Behaviour (OB) is the systematic study of how **individuals, groups and structures** affect behaviour within organisations, applied to make organisations more effective. Its key dependent variables are productivity, absenteeism, turnover, job satisfaction and organisational citizenship behaviour (OCB).

steps.title: Three levels of analysis
steps.body:
- **Individual**: personality, perception, learning, attitudes, motivation.
- **Group**: communication, leadership, power, conflict, teams.
- **Organisation system**: structure, culture, HR policies, change.

steps.title: Contributing disciplines
steps.body:
- **Psychology**: individual learning, personality, motivation.
- **Social psychology**: attitude change, group decision making.
- **Sociology**: groups, formal organisation, culture.
- **Anthropology**: values and cross-cultural differences.
- **Political science**: power and conflict.

steps.title: Systematic study beats intuition
steps.body: Common sense says happy workers are always more productive. Research shows the link is real but moderate, and that productivity can also drive satisfaction. OB asks for evidence rather than gut feel.

steps.title: Why it pays
steps.body: Replacing a mid-level employee commonly costs a substantial fraction of annual salary in hiring and training time. Reducing avoidable turnover through better managers is one of the clearest returns on OB knowledge.

quiz.why: Turnover is an outcome OB tries to explain, while personality, structure and leadership are explanatory variables.

quiz.q: Organisational culture is studied at which level?
quiz.why: Culture is a property of the whole organisation, so it sits at the organisation-system level.

lessons.title: The Hawthorne studies and the human relations movement

scenes.text: At Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago in the 1920s, researchers raised lighting and output went up.
They lowered lighting in the test room and output still went up.
Elton Mayo's team concluded that attention, group norms and social needs mattered more than lighting.

steps.title: Phases of the studies (1924–1932)
steps.body:
- **Illumination experiments**: output rose in both test and control groups.
- **Relay assembly test room**: a small group of women; output rose with almost every change, linked to supervision style and group cohesion.
- **Mass interviewing programme**: about 20,000 interviews revealed workers' feelings.
- **Bank wiring observation room**: men restricted output to an informal group norm.

steps.title: Key conclusions
steps.body: Workers are social beings; informal groups set norms; supervision style and recognition affect output; money is not the only motivator. This launched the **human relations movement**, a reaction to Taylor's purely economic view.

steps.title: The Hawthorne effect
steps.body: People change behaviour because they know they are observed. Modern researchers debate how strong the original effect was, but the term is widely used in research design.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not say Hawthorne proved that lighting has no effect at all. It showed that social and psychological factors could outweigh physical ones in that setting.

quiz.why: Elton Mayo and colleagues from Harvard interpreted the Hawthorne findings and founded the human relations view.

quiz.why: Knowing one is being studied can itself change behaviour, which researchers must control for.

quiz.why: It stressed that recognition, belonging and group norms influence productivity.

lessons.title: Models of OB: autocratic to collegial

scenes.text: In one textile mill the owner says: obey or leave.
In a PSU, generous benefits keep people loyal, but few go beyond the minimum.
In a design studio, the lead treats everyone as a partner and people self-discipline.

steps.title: Keith Davis's four models
steps.body:
- **Autocratic**: basis power; employee orientation obedience; result minimum performance.
- **Custodial**: basis economic resources; orientation security and benefits; result passive cooperation.
- **Supportive**: basis leadership; orientation job performance; result awakened drives.
- **Collegial**: basis partnership; orientation responsible behaviour; result moderate enthusiasm and self-discipline.

steps.title: Classify a case
steps.body: A hospital gives staff housing, pension and canteen but little say in decisions. Staff feel secure yet passive. Basis is economic resources: **custodial** model.

steps.title: No single best model
steps.body: Davis argued the models evolved over time and that organisations often use a mix. A crisis may justify short autocratic phases; knowledge work favours supportive and collegial approaches.

steps.title: Indian context
steps.body: Many family-run SMEs still run autocratically, while IT services and start-ups promote supportive or collegial cultures with flat teams and open feedback.

lessons.title: Personality: Big Five, MBTI and work

scenes.text: Rhea is outgoing and loves cold calls. Kabir is quiet but never misses a follow-up.
After a year both hit target, by different routes.
Their manager learns that personality shapes how people work, not only whether they succeed.

steps.title: Determinants of personality
steps.body: Heredity (genes, temperament), environment (culture, family, education) and situation together shape personality. It is relatively stable but not fixed.

steps.title: Big Five (OCEAN)
steps.body:
- **Openness**: curious, imaginative.
- **Conscientiousness**: organised, dependable: the most consistent predictor of job performance across jobs.
- **Extraversion**: sociable: linked to sales and leadership emergence.
- **Agreeableness**: cooperative, trusting.
- **Neuroticism** (low emotional stability): anxious, linked to lower satisfaction.

steps.title: MBTI
steps.body: Four dichotomies: Extraversion–Introversion, Sensing–Intuition, Thinking–Feeling, Judging–Perceiving, giving 16 types such as ESTJ. Popular in training, but research finds weak validity for selection, so use it for self-awareness only.

steps.title: Other traits used in OB
steps.body: Locus of control (internal vs external), self-monitoring, Machiavellianism, Type A vs Type B, proactive personality.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not use MBTI type to hire or reject. Trait measures support development; selection needs validated tests linked to job requirements.

scenes.text: Sneha reaches the office 20 minutes late. Her manager thinks: she is careless.
When the manager is late, he blames the metro breakdown.
Same event, different explanation. That is attribution bias.

steps.title: Perception
steps.body: Perception is the process of organising and interpreting sensory impressions to give meaning to the environment. Factors: the **perceiver** (attitudes, motives, experience), the **target** (novelty, size, background) and the **situation** (time, setting).

steps.title: Kelley's attribution theory
steps.body:
We judge whether behaviour is internally or externally caused using three cues:
- **Distinctiveness**: does she act this way in other situations?
- **Consensus**: do others act the same way here?
- **Consistency**: does she do this over time?
Low distinctiveness, low consensus, high consistency → internal attribution.

steps.title: Worked case
steps.body: Sneha is late only on Mondays (high distinctiveness), many colleagues are late on Mondays because of a weekly road closure (high consensus), but she is rarely late otherwise (low consistency). Conclusion: **external** cause.

steps.title: Perceptual shortcuts and errors
steps.body:
- **Fundamental attribution error**: overrating internal causes for others.
- **Self-serving bias**: credit for success, blame outside for failure.
- **Halo effect**: one trait colours overall impression.
- **Selective perception**, **contrast effect**, **stereotyping**, **projection**.

steps.title: In appraisals
steps.body: Use specific behaviour records across the whole period to reduce halo and recency effects.

scenes.text: At a Gujarat chemical plant, workers keep removing helmets in the heat.
The supervisor starts praising helmet use and gives a monthly team safety award.
Compliance rises: behaviour followed consequences.

steps.title: Theories of learning
steps.body:
- **Classical conditioning** (Pavlov): association of a neutral stimulus with a reflex response.
- **Operant conditioning** (Skinner): behaviour is a function of its consequences.
- **Social learning** (Bandura): learning by observing models; attention, retention, reproduction, reinforcement.

steps.title: Four ways to shape behaviour
steps.body:
- **Positive reinforcement**: add something pleasant (praise).
- **Negative reinforcement**: remove something unpleasant when behaviour occurs (supervisor stops nagging once report is on time).
- **Punishment**: add an unpleasant consequence (fine).
- **Extinction**: withhold reinforcement so behaviour fades (ignore jokes in meetings).

steps.title: Schedules of reinforcement
steps.body:
- Continuous: every time.
- **Fixed interval**: monthly salary.
- **Variable interval**: surprise audits.
- **Fixed ratio**: piece rate per 100 units.
- **Variable ratio**: commission on uncertain sales, lottery: most resistant to extinction.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Negative reinforcement is not punishment. It **increases** a behaviour by removing something unpleasant.

steps.title: ABC model of attitudes
steps.body:
- **Affective**: feeling (I dislike my supervisor).
- **Behavioural**: intention to act (I will request a transfer).
- **Cognitive**: belief (my supervisor is unfair).

steps.title: Cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957)
steps.body: Discomfort from inconsistency between attitudes or between attitude and behaviour. People reduce it by changing behaviour, changing the attitude, or adding rationalisations. Pressure to reduce it depends on the importance of the elements, perceived control and rewards.

steps.title: Job attitudes and outcomes
steps.body: Job satisfaction, job involvement, organisational commitment (affective, continuance, normative) and employee engagement. Dissatisfaction responses (exit, voice, loyalty, neglect) form the **EVLN** model.

steps.title: Satisfaction and performance
steps.body: The satisfaction–performance correlation is moderate; satisfaction is more strongly linked to lower turnover and absenteeism and to more OCB.

lessons.title: Content theories: Maslow, ERG, Herzberg, McClelland

scenes.text: A Chennai BPO gives every agent a 10% raise to reduce attrition.
Six months later attrition is unchanged. Exit interviews mention no growth and no recognition.
Herzberg would have predicted it: pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create motivation.

steps.title: Maslow's hierarchy (1943)
steps.body: Physiological → safety → social (belongingness) → esteem → self-actualisation. A satisfied need no longer motivates; people move up as lower needs are substantially met. Criticism: little evidence for a strict order.

steps.title: Alderfer's ERG
steps.body: Existence, Relatedness, Growth. Several needs can operate at once, and **frustration–regression**: if growth is blocked, people may regress to relatedness or existence needs (e.g. demand more pay).

steps.title: Herzberg's two-factor theory
steps.body:
- **Hygiene factors** (extrinsic): pay, policy, supervision, working conditions, job security. Absence causes dissatisfaction; presence only brings 'no dissatisfaction'.
- **Motivators** (intrinsic): achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth. Presence creates satisfaction.

steps.title: McClelland's acquired needs
steps.body: nAch (achievement: moderate-risk goals, feedback), nPow (power: influence others), nAff (affiliation: friendly relations). High nAch suits entrepreneurs; effective senior managers often show high socialised nPow and lower nAff.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: In Herzberg, salary is a hygiene factor, not a motivator, even though money matters a great deal to people.

activity.prompt: Hygiene factor or motivator (Herzberg)?

options: blocked higher needs make lower needs more important

quiz.why: Achievers like goals that are hard but attainable and want to know how they are doing.

quiz.q: Which is the top level in Maslow's hierarchy?
quiz.why: Self-actualisation, becoming what one is capable of, sits at the top.

scenes.text: Ankit is offered a trip to Singapore if he sells 120 policies this quarter.
He thinks: can I sell 120? Will the company really give the trip? Do I even want the trip?
Vroom multiplied these three beliefs to predict his effort.

steps.title: The three components
steps.body:
- **Expectancy (E)**: probability effort leads to performance (0 to 1).
- **Instrumentality (I)**: probability performance leads to reward (0 to 1).
- **Valence (V)**: value of the reward (−1 to +1).
Motivational force **MF = E × I × V**. If any component is zero, motivation is zero.

steps.title: Multiple outcomes
steps.body: With several outcomes, MF = E × Σ(I × V). Example: E = 0.7; outcome A (bonus) I = 0.8, V = 0.9; outcome B (longer hours) I = 1.0, V = −0.3. Σ = 0.72 − 0.30 = 0.42. MF = 0.7 × 0.42 = **0.294**.

steps.title: Managerial levers
steps.body: Raise E with training and resources; raise I by keeping promises and transparent rules; raise V by offering rewards people actually value (ask them).

scenes.text: Meera discovers a new hire doing the same job earns ₹8,000 a month more.
She starts leaving exactly at 6 pm and stops mentoring juniors.
She is restoring a sense of balance, as Adams' equity theory predicts.

steps.title: Equity theory (J. Stacy Adams)
steps.body: People compare their outcome/input ratio with a referent's. Inequity (under- or over-reward) causes tension. Responses: change inputs, change outcomes, distort perceptions of self or others, change referent, or leave.

steps.title: Ratio check
steps.body: Meera: outcome ₹50,000, inputs rated 10. Ratio = 5,000. New hire: ₹58,000, inputs rated 8. Ratio = 7,250. Meera's ratio is lower → she feels **under-rewarded**.

steps.title: Organisational justice
steps.body: Distributive (fairness of outcomes), procedural (fairness of process), interactional (respect and information). Procedural justice can soften reactions to unfavourable outcomes.

steps.title: Goal-setting theory (Locke)
steps.body: Specific and difficult goals, when accepted, lead to higher performance than 'do your best' goals. Feedback, commitment, task complexity and self-efficacy moderate the effect.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Hard goals help only if accepted and achievable; impossible goals reduce commitment and can encourage unethical shortcuts.

lessons.title: Job design and the Job Characteristics Model

scenes.text: Insurance clerks each check one field of a claim form, all day.
The firm redesigns: each clerk owns whole claims for a set of customers and gets feedback on settlement time.
Absenteeism drops. They boosted the job's core characteristics.

steps.title: Hackman & Oldham's five core dimensions
steps.body: Skill variety (SV), task identity (TI), task significance (TS), autonomy (A), feedback (F). They create critical psychological states: meaningfulness, responsibility, knowledge of results.

steps.title: Motivating Potential Score
steps.body:
MPS = ((SV + TI + TS) / 3) × A × F, each on a 1–7 scale.
Old clerk job: SV 2, TI 1, TS 4, A 2, F 2. MPS = (7/3) × 2 × 2 = 2.333 × 4 = **9.33**.
Redesigned: SV 5, TI 6, TS 4, A 5, F 6. MPS = (15/3) × 5 × 6 = 5 × 30 = **150**.

steps.title: Job design options
steps.body:
- **Job rotation**: move between tasks.
- **Job enlargement**: add more tasks at the same level (horizontal).
- **Job enrichment**: add planning and control responsibility (vertical).
- Alternative arrangements: flexitime, job sharing, telework.

steps.title: Why autonomy and feedback matter most
steps.body: They multiply the score, so a job with zero autonomy or zero feedback scores very low no matter how varied it is.

scenes.text: Five people from sales, design and finance form a squad to launch a millet snack.
Week three: arguments about price and packaging.
By week eight they have agreed roles and ship on time. Classic Tuckman.

steps.title: Types of groups
steps.body:
- **Formal**: command group (manager and reports), task group (cross-functional for a job).
- **Informal**: interest group, friendship group.
People join for security, status, self-esteem, affiliation, power and goal achievement.

steps.title: Tuckman's five stages
steps.body: **Forming** (uncertainty) → **Storming** (conflict over control) → **Norming** (cohesion, shared norms) → **Performing** (focused on task) → **Adjourning** (wrap-up for temporary groups). The punctuated-equilibrium model notes that temporary groups often change direction sharply around the midpoint of their deadline.

steps.title: Group properties
steps.body: Roles (role conflict, role ambiguity), norms (Asch conformity), status, size (groups above about 7 see more social loafing) and cohesiveness. High cohesiveness with high performance norms gives the highest productivity; high cohesiveness with low norms gives the lowest.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Cohesion is not automatically good. A tight group can unite against management goals.

lessons.title: Group decision making: groupthink, loafing and techniques

scenes.text: A board unanimously approves an expensive acquisition in one meeting.
Two directors had doubts but stayed silent to keep harmony.
Within a year the deal is written off. That is groupthink.

steps.title: Groupthink (Janis)
steps.body: Symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, belief in inherent morality, stereotyping outsiders, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, self-appointed mindguards.

steps.title: Other pitfalls
steps.body:
- **Social loafing**: less effort in groups (Ringelmann's rope-pulling). Fix: make individual contributions identifiable.
- **Group shift / polarisation**: group decision becomes more extreme than members' initial positions.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **Brainstorming**: no criticism, quantity first.
- **Nominal group technique**: silent idea writing, round-robin sharing, discussion, private ranking.
- **Delphi**: anonymous experts answer questionnaires in rounds with feedback.
- **Devil's advocate**: someone is assigned to challenge the proposal.

steps.title: Leaders speak last
steps.body: When the senior person states a view first, others anchor on it. Asking juniors first reduces conformity.

steps.title: Group vs team
steps.body: A work group shares information; performance is the sum of individual inputs. A work team generates **positive synergy** through coordinated effort, shared accountability and complementary skills.

steps.title: Types of teams
steps.body: Problem-solving teams (quality circles), self-managed work teams, cross-functional teams, virtual teams, multiteam systems.

steps.title: What makes teams effective
steps.body:
- **Context**: resources, leadership, trust, fair rewards.
- **Composition**: abilities, personality mix, roles, diversity, size (often 5–9).
- **Process**: common purpose, specific goals, team efficacy, managed conflict, low social loafing.

steps.title: The process
steps.body: Sender → encoding → message → channel → decoding → receiver → feedback, with **noise** possible at every stage.

steps.title: Directions and networks
steps.body: Downward, upward, lateral. Small-group networks: **chain** (accuracy, rigid), **wheel** (fast, central leader), **all-channel** (high satisfaction, good for complex tasks). The **grapevine** is informal, fast, and often largely accurate, but it spreads rumours when official information is missing.

steps.title: Barriers
steps.body: Filtering, selective perception, information overload, emotions, language/jargon, silence, communication apprehension, cultural differences, and channel mismatch (bad news by email).

steps.title: Channel richness
steps.body: Face-to-face is the richest channel; use it for ambiguous or emotional messages. Use lean channels (memos, emails) for routine information.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Leadership, Power and Politics
courses.summary: Trait, behavioural and contingency theories of leadership (Ohio State, Michigan, Managerial Grid, Fiedler, Hersey–Blanchard, path–goal), transformational and servant leadership, French and Raven's bases of power, and organisational politics.

steps.title: Trait theories

steps.title: Ohio State and Michigan studies

- Michigan: **employee-oriented** vs **production-oriented** leaders; employee orientation linked to higher productivity and satisfaction.

steps.title: Blake & Mouton Managerial Grid
steps.body: Concern for people (1–9) vs concern for production (1–9): 1,1 impoverished; 1,9 country club; 9,1 task (authority-compliance); 5,5 middle-of-the-road; 9,9 team management (considered ideal).

steps.title: Common mistake

scenes.text: Tanvi leads fresh graduates, mid-level engineers and senior architects.

steps.title: Fiedler's contingency model
steps.body: Style is fixed, measured by the **LPC** (least preferred co-worker) scale: high LPC = relationship-oriented, low LPC = task-oriented. Situation favourableness: leader–member relations, task structure, position power. Task-oriented leaders do best in **very favourable or very unfavourable** situations; relationship-oriented leaders in moderate ones. Fix: change the situation or the leader.

steps.title: Hersey–Blanchard situational leadership
steps.body:
Follower readiness R1–R4 → style:
- R1 (unable, unwilling) → **Telling** (S1)
- R2 (unable, willing) → **Selling** (S2)
- R3 (able, unwilling) → **Participating** (S3)
- R4 (able, willing) → **Delegating** (S4)

steps.title: House's path–goal theory
steps.body: Leaders clarify the path to goals and remove obstacles. Styles: directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented, chosen according to employee and task contingencies (e.g. directive helps with ambiguous tasks, less so for experienced staff).

steps.title: Apply it
steps.body: Senior architects are able but demotivated after a reorganisation: R3. Best style: **participating**: share ideas, facilitate decisions, little task direction.

scenes.text: A loss-making public-sector unit gets a new CMD.
He shares a clear vision, visits every shift, and asks workers for ideas.

steps.title: Transactional leadership
steps.body: Exchange-based: contingent reward and management by exception (active or passive). Clarifies roles and rewards targets.

steps.title: Transformational leadership (Bass): the four I's
steps.body:
- **Idealised influence** (role model, charisma)
- **Inspirational motivation** (vision)
- **Intellectual stimulation** (challenge assumptions)
- **Individualised consideration** (coach each person)

steps.title: Other contemporary approaches
steps.body:
- **Servant leadership** (Greenleaf): serve followers' growth first.
- **Authentic and ethical leadership**: self-awareness, transparency.
- **Leader–member exchange (LMX)**: in-groups and out-groups.

steps.title: Not either/or
steps.body: Transformational leadership builds on a transactional base; good leaders use both.

steps.title: French & Raven's bases of power
steps.body:
- **Formal**: legitimate (position), reward, coercive.
- **Personal**: expert, referent (admiration, charisma).
Information power is often added. Personal power correlates more with commitment; coercive power with resistance.

steps.title: Dependency
steps.body: Power is a function of dependency: the more important, scarce and non-substitutable the resource you control, the more power you hold.

steps.title: Political behaviour
steps.body: Activities not required by the role that influence the distribution of advantages: coalitions, impression management, withholding information. More common with scarce resources, ambiguous goals, unclear performance measures and zero-sum rewards.

steps.title: Ethics test
steps.body: Ask: what is the purpose (self-serving or organisational)? Does it respect others' rights? Is it fair?

courses.title: Unit 6 · Conflict, Culture, Change and Stress
courses.summary: Conflict views and Thomas–Kilmann handling styles, organisational culture (Schein's levels, strong vs weak cultures), Lewin's and Kotter's change models, resistance to change, and work stress and its management.
outcomes: Explain traditional, human relations and interactionist views of conflict

scenes.text: Sales promises a client delivery in 7 days.
Production says 15 days is the minimum without overtime.

steps.title: Views of conflict
steps.body:
- **Traditional**: all conflict is harmful.
- **Human relations**: conflict is natural and inevitable.
- **Interactionist**: some functional conflict keeps groups self-critical and creative. Task conflict at low-to-moderate levels can help; relationship conflict is almost always dysfunctional.

steps.title: Thomas–Kilmann modes
steps.body:
Based on assertiveness and cooperativeness:
- **Competing** (high A, low C)
- **Collaborating** (high A, high C)
- **Compromising** (middle)
- **Avoiding** (low A, low C)
- **Accommodating** (low A, high C)

steps.title: Negotiation
steps.body: **Distributive** bargaining divides a fixed pie (win–lose); **integrative** bargaining expands the pie (win–win). Know your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) and your reservation point.

steps.title: Bargaining zone
steps.body: Buyer will pay up to ₹12 lakh; seller will accept no less than ₹10 lakh. Zone of possible agreement = ₹10–12 lakh, a range of ₹2 lakh.

steps.title: Schein's three levels
steps.body:
- **Artifacts**: visible structures, dress, rituals, office layout.
- **Espoused values**: stated strategies, goals, philosophies.
- **Basic underlying assumptions**: unconscious, taken-for-granted beliefs, the real source of values and action.

steps.title: Strong vs weak cultures
steps.body: In a strong culture core values are intensely held and widely shared, giving behavioural control and lower turnover, but also resistance to change and to diversity.

steps.title: How culture is created and sustained
steps.body: Founders' values → selection → top management behaviour → socialisation (pre-arrival, encounter, metamorphosis). Culture is learned through stories, rituals, material symbols and language.

steps.title: Indian examples
steps.body: Many long-established Indian groups publicly emphasise trust and community values, while newer tech firms highlight speed and ownership. Students should treat such statements as espoused values and look for artifacts that confirm or contradict them.

scenes.text: A district cooperative bank decides to move all loan files to a digital system.
Senior clerks resist: they fear looking incompetent.
The manager explains why, trains them and celebrates the first branch to go live.

steps.title: Lewin's three-step model
steps.body: **Unfreezing** (create readiness, reduce restraining forces) → **Movement/Change** → **Refreezing** (stabilise via rewards and policies). Force-field analysis lists driving vs restraining forces.

steps.title: Kotter's eight steps
steps.body: 1 Create urgency 2 Form a guiding coalition 3 Create a vision 4 Communicate the vision 5 Empower others/remove obstacles 6 Create short-term wins 7 Consolidate gains 8 Anchor changes in culture.

steps.title: Resistance and how to handle it
steps.body: Sources: habit, security, economic fears, fear of the unknown, selective information processing, group inertia, threatened power. Tactics: education and communication, participation, support, negotiation, manipulation/co-optation (risky), coercion (last resort).

steps.title: Force-field scoring
steps.body: Driving forces: RBI compliance (5), faster loan approval (4), cost saving (3) = 12. Restraining: fear of tech (4), training time (3), job worry (4) = 11. Driving exceeds restraining by 1; reducing restraints (training) is usually more effective than adding pressure.

scenes.text: An audit associate works 14-hour days for three weeks at quarter end.

steps.title: Stress and its types
steps.body: Stress is a dynamic condition in which a person faces an opportunity, demand or resource related to something desired whose outcome is uncertain and important. **Challenge stressors** (deadlines, responsibility) differ from **hindrance stressors** (red tape, role ambiguity).

steps.title: Sources
steps.body:
- **Environmental**: economic, political, technological uncertainty.
- **Organisational**: task demands, role demands, interpersonal demands.
- **Personal**: family, financial problems, personality (Type A).

steps.title: Consequences and the GAS model
steps.body: Physiological (blood pressure, headaches), psychological (anxiety, dissatisfaction), behavioural (absenteeism, turnover). Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion.

steps.title: Managing stress
steps.body: Individual: time management, exercise, relaxation, social support. Organisational: better selection and job design, clear goals, employee assistance programmes, wellness programmes, flexible work.

uni-bba-operations-management.title: BBA · Operations Management
uni-bba-operations-management.description: Operations management for BBA: production systems, productivity, demand forecasting, facility location and layout, capacity planning, aggregate planning and scheduling, inventory and MRP, project scheduling with CPM/PERT, quality control charts, TQM, Six Sigma, lean and supply chain basics, with solved numericals. courses.title: Unit 1 · Operations, productivity and forecasting
courses.summary: The transformation model, goods versus services, types of production systems, single and multifactor productivity, and demand forecasting with moving averages, exponential smoothing, least-squares trend and error measures.
outcomes: Describe operations as an input-transformation-output system

lessons.title: Nature and scope of operations management

scenes.text: A Bengaluru café chain buys beans, milk and labour hours, and turns them into coffee and an experience.
The kitchen, the queue and the delivery app are all part of its operations system.

steps.title: Definition and transformation model
steps.body: Operations management (OM) is the design, operation and improvement of the systems that create and deliver a firm's goods and services. Model: **inputs** (materials, labour, capital, information, energy) → **transformation** (physical, locational, exchange, storage, physiological, informational) → **outputs** (goods, services), with feedback and control. Objectives: cost, quality, speed, dependability, flexibility.

steps.title: Goods versus services
steps.body: Services are intangible, produced and consumed simultaneously, perishable (an empty seat cannot be stored), heterogeneous and involve high customer contact. Hence capacity and queue management matter more than inventory in services.

steps.title: Types of production systems
steps.body: **Job (project) production**: one-off, customised (ship, wedding catering). **Batch**: groups of identical items (bakery, pharmaceuticals). **Mass/flow**: high volume, standard items on lines (two-wheelers). **Continuous/process**: non-stop flow (refinery, cement). Moving from job to continuous: volume rises, variety falls, equipment becomes special-purpose.

steps.title: Historical milestones
steps.body: Division of labour (Adam Smith, 1776), interchangeable parts (Eli Whitney), scientific management (Taylor, 1911), moving assembly line (Ford, 1913), Hawthorne studies, statistical quality control (Shewhart), Toyota Production System and lean, and today's Industry 4.0 with IoT and analytics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a restaurant 'non-operations': services have operations too.
- Confusing batch production with mass production: batch switches products between runs.

activity.prompt: Classify each production system

quiz.why: An empty hotel room tonight cannot be sold tomorrow, so capacity matching is critical.

quiz.q: A cement plant is an example of
quiz.why: It runs around the clock with a standard product flowing through fixed process equipment.

scenes.text: A Ludhiana bicycle unit makes 1,200 frames using 300 labour hours this week.
The owner wants a number to compare weeks and plants.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Productivity = Output ÷ Input**. Partial (single-factor): output per labour hour, per machine hour, per kg material. **Multifactor** = output ÷ (labour + material + capital + energy) in money terms. **Total factor** uses all inputs. Productivity growth % = (current − previous) ÷ previous × 100. Efficiency = actual output ÷ standard output; effectiveness = doing the right things.

steps.title: Worked example 1: labour productivity
steps.body:
1,200 frames ÷ 300 hours = **4 frames per labour hour**.
Next week: 1,380 frames in 300 hours = 4.6. Growth = (4.6 − 4)/4 = **15%**.

steps.title: Worked example 2: multifactor
steps.body:
Output value ₹2,40,000. Inputs: labour ₹40,000, material ₹1,00,000, overhead ₹20,000 = ₹1,60,000.
Multifactor productivity = 2,40,000 ÷ 1,60,000 = **1.5**.

steps.title: Ways to improve
steps.body: Better methods (work study), training, automation, lean waste elimination, maintenance to cut downtime, better layout, and motivation. Productivity in services is harder to measure because output quality varies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing units in multifactor productivity (hours plus rupees).
- Treating production volume as productivity: more output with more input may mean no gain.

lessons.title: Forecasting: qualitative methods and moving averages

scenes.text: The café's demand was 120, 130, 110 and 140 thousand cups in four months.
The purchase head must order beans for month 5 today.

steps.title: Types of forecasts
steps.body: Time horizons: short (up to 3 months), medium (3 months–2 years), long (beyond 2 years). **Qualitative**: jury of executive opinion, sales-force composite, Delphi method (anonymous expert rounds), market survey. **Quantitative**: time series (naive, moving average, exponential smoothing, trend projection) and causal (regression). Demand components: trend, seasonality, cycles, random variation.

steps.title: Worked example 1: simple moving average
steps.body:
3-month MA for month 5 = (130 + 110 + 140) ÷ 3 = **126.67** thousand cups.
Naive forecast would be the last value, 140.

steps.title: Worked example 2: weighted moving average
steps.body:
Weights 0.5 (latest), 0.3, 0.2.
F₅ = 0.5 × 140 + 0.3 × 110 + 0.2 × 130 = 70 + 33 + 26 = **129** thousand cups.
Weights must add to 1; heavier recent weights react faster.

steps.title: Choosing n
steps.body: A larger n gives a smoother but slower-reacting forecast; a smaller n reacts faster but follows noise. Moving averages lag behind a trend.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including the month being forecast in the average.
- Using weights that do not sum to 1.

steps.title: Exponential smoothing

steps.title: Measuring error

steps.title: Line balancing
steps.body: **Cycle time C = available time ÷ required output**. **Minimum stations = Σt ÷ C** (round up). Assign tasks respecting precedence and C (e.g. longest task first). **Efficiency = Σt ÷ (N × C)**; balance delay = 1 − efficiency.

steps.title: If a task exceeds C
steps.body: Duplicate the station, split the task, or use overtime; otherwise output target cannot be met.

lessons.title: Aggregate planning and the master schedule

scenes.text: A raincoat maker expects 800, 1,200, 1,000 and 1,000 units over four months.

steps.title: Hierarchy of planning
steps.body: Long-range (capacity, facilities) → **aggregate plan** (medium term, 3–18 months, product families, workforce and output levels) → **master production schedule** (which end items, how many, when) → MRP and shop-floor scheduling (short term).

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body: **Level**: constant output; inventory absorbs swings (stable workforce, holding cost). **Chase**: output follows demand by hiring/layoffs or overtime (low inventory, hiring and firing cost, morale). **Mixed**: combine levers such as overtime, subcontracting, part-time labour, backorders. Demand-side options: pricing, promotions, complementary products.

steps.title: Worked example: level plan
steps.body:
Total demand = 4,000 over 4 months → level output 1,000/month.
Ending inventory: M1 = 1,000 − 800 = 200; M2 = 200 + 1,000 − 1,200 = 0; M3 = 0; M4 = 0.
Holding cost at ₹5 per unit-month = 200 × 5 = **₹1,000**. Under a chase plan holding cost is 0, but output must rise by 400 then fall by 200, incurring hiring and layoff costs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating aggregate planning as item-level scheduling.
- Ignoring a shortage under a level plan if early demand is high (check cumulative production ≥ cumulative demand).

steps.title: Priority rules (single machine)
steps.body: FCFS (first come), **SPT** (shortest processing time: minimises average flow time), **EDD** (earliest due date: minimises maximum lateness), critical ratio = time to due date ÷ work remaining. Measures: average flow time, average tardiness, number of late jobs, utilisation.

steps.title: Worked example 1: SPT vs FCFS
steps.body:
Jobs (days, due): A (6, 8), B (2, 6), C (8, 18), D (3, 15), E (9, 23).
FCFS A-B-C-D-E: completions 6, 8, 16, 19, 28 → average flow 77/5 = 15.4; tardiness 0, 2, 0, 4, 5 → average 2.2.
SPT B-D-A-C-E: completions 2, 5, 11, 19, 28 → average flow 65/5 = **13**; tardiness 0, 0, 3, 1, 5 → average **1.8**.

steps.title: Johnson's rule (n jobs, 2 machines)
steps.body: Find the smallest time in the list. If it is on machine 1, place the job as early as possible; if on machine 2, as late as possible. Remove the job and repeat. Minimises makespan.

steps.title: Worked example 2: Johnson

B (1 on M1) first; A (2 on M2) last; D (3 on M1) second; E (4 on M2) fourth; C third → **B-D-C-E-A**.
M1 finishes: 1, 4, 13, 23, 28. M2: B 1–7, D 7–15, C 15–22, E 23–27, A 28–30. **Makespan 30 h**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting a job on M2 before it finishes on M1.
- Counting negative lateness as tardiness (tardiness is never negative).

steps.title: Independent vs dependent demand
steps.body: Finished goods have independent demand (forecast) → EOQ and reorder point. Components have dependent demand (calculated from the MPS) → MRP. **ROP = demand during lead time + safety stock = d × L + SS**. Safety stock with variable demand ≈ z × σ_d × √L.

steps.title: Worked example 1: reorder point

steps.title: MRP logic
steps.body: Inputs: MPS, bill of materials (BOM), inventory records. Steps for each item: gross requirement → subtract on-hand and scheduled receipts → **net requirement** → lot size → offset by lead time → **planned order release**. Outputs: planned orders, reschedule notices. MRP II adds capacity and finance; ERP extends to the whole enterprise.

steps.title: Worked example 2: MRP explosion
steps.body:
200 bikes in week 6; 2 wheels each → gross 400 wheels in week 6.
On hand 50 → net = **350**.
Lead time 2 weeks → planned order release of 350 wheels in **week 4**. Each wheel needs 36 spokes → 12,600 spokes needed by week 4.

steps.body:

- Forgetting lead-time offset.

steps.title: CPM concepts
steps.body: Network of activities with durations and precedence. Forward pass: ES, EF = ES + t. Backward pass: LF, LS = LF − t. **Total float = LS − ES**. Critical path: longest path, activities with zero float; its length is project duration.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
A (3) start; B (4) start; C (2) after A; D (6) after A; E (3) after B, C; F (2) after D, E.
Paths: A-C-E-F = 10; A-D-F = **11**; B-E-F = 9. Duration 11 days; critical path A-D-F.
Forward: E's ES = max(5, 4) = 5. Backward: F LS = 9; E LF = 9, LS = 6; C LF = 6, LS = 4 (ES 3) → float 1; B LF = 6, LS = 2 → float **2**.

steps.title: PERT
steps.body: Three estimates: optimistic a, most likely m, pessimistic b. **tₑ = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6**; **σ = (b − a) ÷ 6**. Project variance = sum of variances on the critical path; Z = (T − Tₑ) ÷ σ_project for probability of completion by T.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body:
a = 2, m = 5, b = 14 → tₑ = (2 + 20 + 14) ÷ 6 = **6 days**; σ = 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
If critical-path Tₑ = 20 and σ = 2, P(finish ≤ 22) → Z = 1 → about **84%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the shortest path as critical.
- Adding standard deviations instead of variances.

steps.title: Dimensions and costs
steps.body: Garvin's dimensions: performance, features, reliability, conformance, durability, serviceability, aesthetics, perceived quality. **Cost of quality**: prevention (training, design reviews), appraisal (inspection, testing), internal failure (scrap, rework), external failure (warranty, returns, lost goodwill). Spending on prevention usually reduces total cost.

steps.title: Gurus and TQM

TQM = customer focus, continuous improvement (kaizen), employee involvement, process approach, fact-based decisions. ISO 9001 specifies requirements for a quality management system.

steps.title: Six Sigma
steps.body: Aims at 3.4 defects per million opportunities (with the conventional 1.5σ shift). **DPMO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit) × 10⁶**. Method **DMAIC**: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control. Roles: Champion, Master Black Belt, Black Belt, Green Belt.

steps.body: Lean (from the Toyota Production System) maximises value by eliminating waste (muda). Seven wastes, TIMWOOD: **T**ransport, **I**nventory, **M**otion, **W**aiting, **O**verproduction, **O**ver-processing, **D**efects (often an 8th: unused talent). Tools: value stream mapping, 5S (sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain), SMED for quick changeovers, poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), jidoka, kaizen, heijunka (levelling).

steps.title: JIT and kanban
steps.body: Just-in-time produces and delivers only what is needed, when needed, in the quantity needed: pull system, small lots, reliable suppliers, preventive maintenance. Kanban cards signal replenishment. **Number of kanbans = d × L × (1 + α) ÷ C** (d demand rate, L lead time, α safety factor, C container size).

story.title: Why do orders swing so wildly?

scenes.text: A juice brand sees retail sales rise 5%, yet its bottle supplier receives orders up 40%.
Each stage over-reacts: the bullwhip effect.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: A supply chain links suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and customers through material, information and money flows. Drivers (Chopra and Meindl): facilities, inventory, transportation, information, sourcing, pricing. Strategy fit: efficient chains for functional products; responsive chains for innovative products (Fisher). Make-or-buy, vendor selection and vendor-managed inventory are key decisions.

steps.title: Bullwhip effect
steps.body: Small changes in consumer demand amplify upstream. Causes: demand forecast updating at each stage, order batching, price fluctuations and promotions, rationing and shortage gaming. Remedies: share point-of-sale data, reduce lead times, everyday low pricing, VMI, collaborative planning (CPFR).

steps.title: Indian context
steps.body: GST (2017) reduced the need for state-wise warehouses and enabled hub-based networks; e-way bills track goods movement. Logistics improvements such as dedicated freight corridors aim to lower transport cost.

steps.title: Worked example: inventory turnover
steps.body:
Cost of goods sold ₹60 lakh; average inventory ₹10 lakh.
Turnover = 60 ÷ 10 = **6 times a year**; days of inventory = 365 ÷ 6 ≈ **61 days**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blaming the bullwhip only on customers: it is created inside the chain.

lessons.title: Meaning of strategy and levels of strategy

scenes.text: At a diversified Indian group, the board debates whether to enter renewable energy.
The cement division head debates how to beat rivals in the south; the marketing team debates the dealer scheme.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Chandler (1962): strategy is the determination of the basic long-term goals of an enterprise and the adoption of courses of action and allocation of resources necessary to carry them out. Porter: strategy is about being different, choosing a unique and valuable position and making trade-offs. **Strategic management** is the continuous process of formulating, implementing and evaluating cross-functional decisions that enable an organisation to achieve its objectives.

steps.title: Levels of strategy
steps.body: **Corporate level**: what businesses to be in, resource allocation across them (diversify, acquire, exit). **Business level (SBU)**: how to compete in a given market (cost leadership, differentiation, focus). **Functional level**: how each function (marketing, operations, HR, finance) supports the business strategy. A strategic business unit (SBU) is a unit with its own market, competitors and strategy.

steps.title: Characteristics of strategic decisions
steps.body: Long-term, affect the whole organisation, involve significant resources, are often irreversible, deal with uncertainty, and require top-management involvement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a tactic (a discount scheme) as a strategy.
- Mixing corporate questions (which industries) with business questions (how to compete).

steps.title: Mintzberg's 5 Ps
steps.body: Strategy as **Plan** (consciously intended course), **Ploy** (manoeuvre to outwit a rival), **Pattern** (consistency in behaviour over time), **Position** (place in the environment) and **Perspective** (the organisation's way of seeing the world).

steps.title: Deliberate vs emergent
steps.body: **Intended** strategy is planned. Part may be **unrealised**. **Deliberate** strategy is the intended strategy actually implemented. **Emergent** strategy arises from actions and learning without being planned. **Realised strategy = deliberate + emergent**. Effective firms combine planning with learning.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: Intended: 70% sales via retail chains. Realised after two years: 60% online, 30% retail, 10% corporate gifting. The online focus is emergent; managers later formalise it into the plan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating emergent strategy as failure: it is often adaptive learning.
- Forgetting 'perspective', the cultural lens of a firm.

steps.title: Stages

steps.title: Models
steps.body: Glueck and Jauch, Thompson and Strickland, Wheelen and Hunger, and David's comprehensive model all share these stages. Strategic planning can be formal (annual cycle) or continuous.

steps.title: Strategists
steps.body: Board of directors, CEO and top management, SBU heads, corporate planning staff, consultants, and middle managers who implement and feed back. Benefits: proactive stance, alignment, resource focus; limitations: cost, rigidity, analysis paralysis.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Treating the process as one-way; evaluation feeds back into intent and formulation.
- Ignoring implementation, where most strategies fail.

steps.title: Vision and mission

steps.title: Goals and objectives
steps.body: Goals are broad; objectives are specific, measurable and time-bound (SMART), e.g. 'raise EBITDA margin from 14% to 17% by FY2028'. Hierarchy: vision → mission → goals → objectives → strategies → policies.

The board approves strategy, monitors management and manages risk.

lessons.title: Five forces, concentration and industry life cycle

steps.title: Porter's five forces
steps.body: 1 **Threat of new entrants** (barriers: scale, capital, brand, regulation, access to distribution). 2 **Bargaining power of suppliers** (concentration, switching costs). 3 **Bargaining power of buyers** (price sensitivity, information, switching). 4 **Threat of substitutes** (price-performance of alternatives). 5 **Rivalry** (number and balance of rivals, growth, fixed costs, exit barriers). Strong forces → low industry profitability. Complementors are sometimes added as a sixth force.

steps.title: Worked example: concentration
steps.body:
Five firms with shares 30%, 25%, 20%, 15%, 10%.
**CR4** = 30 + 25 + 20 + 15 = **90%**.
**HHI** = 30² + 25² + 20² + 15² + 10² = 900 + 625 + 400 + 225 + 100 = **2,250** (moderately to highly concentrated by common thresholds).

steps.title: Industry life cycle
steps.body: Introduction (few firms, low sales, high prices), growth (rapid sales, entry), shake-out (consolidation), maturity (slow growth, price competition, efficiency), decline (falling demand, exit or harvest). Strategy shifts from innovation to efficiency over the cycle. Strategic groups cluster firms with similar strategies within an industry.

steps.title: Resource-based view
steps.body: Competitive advantage comes from firm-specific resources (tangible: plant, finance; intangible: brand, patents, culture) and capabilities (ability to deploy resources). Barney's **VRIO**: is it **V**aluable, **R**are, costly to **I**mitate, and is the firm **O**rganised to exploit it? V only → parity; V + R → temporary advantage; V + R + I + O → sustained competitive advantage.

steps.title: Value chain (Porter)
steps.body: **Primary activities**: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service. **Support activities**: firm infrastructure, HR management, technology development, procurement. Margin = value created − cost of activities. Analyse each activity for cost drivers and differentiation sources, and linkages between them.

steps.title: Core competence (Prahalad and Hamel, 1990)
steps.body: A core competence provides access to many markets, contributes significantly to customer benefits, and is hard to imitate. Examples often cited: Honda's engines, Sony's miniaturisation. Firms should build and leverage competences across products.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Calling any strength a core competence.

steps.title: Porter's generic strategies
steps.body: **Cost leadership**: lowest cost in the industry through scale, learning, process efficiency, tight cost control; sell at or near industry price for higher margin, or lower price for share. **Differentiation**: unique attributes valued by customers (quality, brand, service, design) that justify a premium. **Focus**: serve a narrow segment with cost focus or differentiation focus. Porter warned of being 'stuck in the middle' without a clear advantage.

steps.title: Risks
steps.body: Cost leadership: technological change, imitation, losing sight of customer needs. Differentiation: premium too high, imitation, buyers stop valuing the difference. Focus: segment shrinks, broad rivals target it.

steps.title: Bowman's strategy clock
steps.body: Eight positions by price and perceived value: low price/low value, low price, hybrid (low price, high value), differentiation, focused differentiation, and failure positions (increased price/standard value, high price/low value, low value/standard price). Hybrid strategies show that some firms combine cost and value through operations excellence.

steps.title: Indian examples (illustrative)
steps.body: Cost leadership: low-cost airlines with single aircraft type and quick turnarounds. Differentiation: premium paint brands offering colour consultancy and tinting. Focus: a hospital chain specialising only in eye care.

steps.title: Grand strategies (Glueck)
steps.body: **Expansion/growth**, **stability**, **retrenchment**, and **combination**. Growth routes: intensification (Ansoff: penetration, market development, product development), **integration** (vertical: backward towards suppliers, forward towards customers; horizontal: acquiring rivals), **diversification** (related/concentric, unrelated/conglomerate), and **internationalisation**.

steps.title: Retrenchment
steps.body: **Turnaround** (cost cutting, asset reduction, revenue generation to reverse decline), **divestment** (sell a business unit), **liquidation** (close and sell assets). Also captive company strategy (becoming a dedicated supplier) and harvesting.

steps.title: Stability
steps.body: Continue in the same business with incremental improvement: pause/proceed with caution, no change, or profit strategy. Suitable in mature, stable environments or after rapid growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling buying a supplier 'forward integration' (it is backward).
- Treating diversification as always good; unrelated diversification often destroys value without strong parenting skills.

lessons.title: Mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures and alliances

scenes.text: A domestic insurer considers acquiring a smaller rival, forming a joint venture with a foreign insurer, or building a digital arm itself.
The board asks: does the deal create value for our shareholders?

steps.title: Modes
steps.body: **Merger**: two firms combine into one. **Acquisition**: one firm buys control of another (friendly or hostile). **Joint venture**: partners create a new jointly owned entity. **Strategic alliance**: cooperation without a new entity (licensing, co-marketing, R&D). Choice depends on speed, control, cost, risk and need for partner capabilities.

steps.title: Synergy arithmetic
steps.body: **Synergy = V_AB − (V_A + V_B)**. **Premium** = price paid − V_B. **Acquirer's gain (NPV) = synergy − premium**. Sources: cost synergies (scale, overlap removal), revenue synergies (cross-selling), financial synergies.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: V_A = ₹500 crore, V_B = ₹200 crore, combined value ₹800 crore → synergy = **₹100 crore**. A pays ₹260 crore for B → premium = ₹60 crore. Acquirer's gain = 100 − 60 = **₹40 crore**; B's shareholders gain ₹60 crore.

steps.title: Why deals fail
steps.body: Overpayment (winner's curse), poor integration and culture clash, overestimated synergies, loss of key talent, and distraction from core business.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating total synergy as the acquirer's gain without subtracting the premium.
- Assuming JVs remove all risk: partner conflict is a common reason they end.

lessons.title: Lab: Portfolio analysis with BCG and GE-McKinsey

scenes.text: A group has detergents, biscuits, packaged water and a new plant-based protein brand.
Which should get investment, which should fund others, which should be sold?

steps.title: BCG growth-share matrix
steps.body: Axes: market growth rate (high/low, often 10% cut-off) and **relative market share** = own share ÷ largest rival's share (cut-off 1.0). **Stars** (high growth, high share: invest), **Cash cows** (low growth, high share: harvest cash), **Question marks** (high growth, low share: invest selectively or divest), **Dogs** (low growth, low share: divest or harvest). Cash from cows funds stars and selected question marks.

steps.title: Worked example: BCG placement
steps.body:
Detergents: share 30%, leader rival 15% → RMS 2.0; growth 4% → **cash cow**.
Biscuits: 18% vs 24% → RMS 0.75; growth 6% → **dog**.
Packaged water: 25% vs 20% → RMS 1.25; growth 14% → **star**.
Plant protein: 5% vs 20% → RMS 0.25; growth 30% → **question mark**.

steps.title: GE-McKinsey nine-cell matrix
steps.body: Axes: **industry attractiveness** (market size, growth, profitability, competition, regulation) and **business strength** (share, brand, cost, capabilities), each scored with weights. Cells: invest/grow (top-left), selectivity (diagonal), harvest/divest (bottom-right). More factors than BCG, but more subjective.

steps.title: Worked example: GE score
steps.body: Industry attractiveness factors (weight, score out of 5): growth (0.4, 4), profitability (0.3, 3), competition (0.3, 2). Score = 1.6 + 0.9 + 0.6 = **3.1** (medium-high).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using absolute share instead of relative share in BCG.
- Treating 'dog' as automatic divestment; it may still be profitable or strategically useful.

scenes.text: A bank announced a digital-first strategy, but branches still reward staff for counter transactions.

steps.title: 7S framework
steps.body: Hard S: **Strategy**, **Structure**, **Systems** (processes, IT, incentives). Soft S: **Shared values** (centre), **Style** (leadership), **Staff**, **Skills**. All seven must be aligned; a change in one requires adjustments in others.

steps.title: Structure follows strategy (Chandler)
steps.body: **Simple** (owner-managed start-ups), **functional** (single business, efficiency), **divisional** (by product, geography or customer, for diversified firms), **SBU** structure, **matrix** (dual reporting for projects across functions), **network/virtual** (outsourcing). Mechanistic structures suit stable environments; organic structures suit dynamic ones.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: A single-product cement company uses a functional structure. After diversifying into paints and real estate, it moves to a divisional structure with separate profit centres, keeping finance and HR as shared corporate services.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing strategy without changing incentive systems.
- Using a matrix structure without clear rules for dual reporting.

steps.title: Culture
steps.body: Shared assumptions, values and behaviours. Schein's levels: artefacts, espoused values, basic assumptions. Culture can enable strategy or block it. Leaders shape culture through what they measure, reward, role-model and how they react to crises.

steps.title: Lewin's three-step model
steps.body: **Unfreeze** (create need for change, reduce resistance), **Change/move** (implement new behaviours, structures), **Refreeze** (institutionalise through systems and rewards). Force-field analysis compares driving and restraining forces.

steps.title: Kotter's eight steps
steps.body: 1 Create urgency · 2 Build a guiding coalition · 3 Form a strategic vision · 4 Communicate the vision · 5 Remove obstacles and empower action · 6 Generate short-term wins · 7 Sustain acceleration · 8 Institute change in culture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring victory too early (Kotter's warning).
- Ignoring informal leaders who shape opinion.

lessons.title: Lab: Strategic control and the balanced scorecard

scenes.text: A hospital chain's profits rose, but patient satisfaction and nurse retention fell.
A balanced scorecard shows the full picture.

steps.title: Types of strategic control
steps.body: **Premise control**: checks whether planning assumptions (demand, policy) still hold. **Implementation control**: monitors milestones and projects. **Strategic surveillance**: broad scanning for unexpected events. **Special alert control**: rapid response to sudden crises (pandemic, plant fire). Operational control uses budgets, variances and KPIs.

steps.title: Balanced scorecard (Kaplan and Norton)
steps.body: Four perspectives: **Financial** (ROCE, revenue growth), **Customer** (satisfaction, retention, share), **Internal processes** (cycle time, quality), **Learning and growth** (skills, retention, IT capability). Objectives are linked in a **strategy map**: learning drives processes, processes drive customer outcomes, which drive financial results.

steps.title: Worked example: weighted score
steps.body:
Weights and achievement vs target: financial 0.30 × 90%; customer 0.25 × 80%; process 0.25 × 100%; learning 0.20 × 70%.
Score = 27 + 20 + 25 + 14 = **86%**.

steps.title: Worked example: variance
steps.body: Target ROCE 18%, actual 15%. Shortfall = 3 percentage points = 3 ÷ 18 = **16.7%** of target → investigate whether the cause is premise (demand) or implementation (cost overrun).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using only lagging financial measures.
- Too many KPIs with no causal links.

steps.title: Blue ocean strategy (Kim and Mauborgne)
steps.body: Red oceans: existing markets with fierce competition. Blue oceans: uncontested market space created by **value innovation** (raising value while lowering cost). **ERRC grid**: Eliminate, Reduce, Raise, Create factors. Strategy canvas plots competing factors against offering level. Classic case: Cirque du Soleil.

steps.title: Digital and platform strategy
steps.body: Platforms create value by connecting user groups (network effects); data and ecosystems become strategic assets. India's digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, ONDC) has lowered entry barriers for platforms.

steps.title: Sustainability and ESG
steps.body: Strategy increasingly integrates environmental, social and governance factors. Large listed companies in India publish the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) under SEBI rules. CSR spending is mandated for companies above thresholds under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating blue ocean with only a new product; it is a new value-cost combination.
- Treating ESG as public relations rather than risk and opportunity.

scenes.text: The exam case: a regional jewellery chain faces national brands entering its towns.
A step-by-step method turns facts into a defensible recommendation.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1 Read and identify the core problem · 2 Situation analysis (PESTEL, five forces, internal strengths/weaknesses) · 3 Generate 2–3 alternatives · 4 Evaluate them on criteria (fit, feasibility, acceptability, risk) · 5 Recommend one with justification · 6 Implementation plan and control measures.

steps.title: Case facts
steps.body: The chain has 22 stores in tier-2 towns, strong local trust, family-run management, limited online presence. National brands offer certified purity (hallmarking), EMI options and digital catalogues. Gold prices are volatile; younger buyers prefer lightweight daily-wear designs.

steps.title: Model answer outline
steps.body: Problem: defend share against branded entrants. Alternatives: (a) price war, (b) differentiation through local designs, hallmarked purity guarantees and personalised service plus omnichannel, (c) sell to a national brand. Evaluation: (a) erodes margins, (b) uses strengths (trust, local insight) and fixes weakness (digital), (c) premature. Recommend (b); implement with a professional COO, design studio, online catalogue and EMI partnerships; control through balanced scorecard (repeat customers, footfall conversion, margin).

steps.title: Evaluation criteria
steps.body: Suitability (fits the situation), feasibility (resources available) and acceptability (to stakeholders: returns, risk, reactions) — Johnson, Scholes and Whittington's SFA criteria.
